lead: Hydrographic surveying measures depth and position in water bodies. Underground surveying carries surface coordinates and direction below ground. Both extend control beyond dry land: one through water, one down a shaft. An echo sounder turns two-way sound travel time into depth. Tide reduction converts that depth to chart datum. GNSS or a total station fixes each sounding. Underground, a shaft transfers coordinates and azimuth to a tunnel traverse. Ports, dredging, dams and metro tunnels use it.
prereq: You need total station: components, working and errors, GPS and GNSS: principles and positioning methods and levelling for heights and control.

blocks.text: An echo sounder has a transducer under the boat. It sends a short sound pulse down and receives the echo from the bed. The timer records the two-way travel time t. The pulse goes down and back, so one-way path is half the total. A transducer converts electrical energy to sound and back. The bed gives a strong echo.

blocks.where: d is depth below the transducer in metres, c is sound speed in the water in m/s, and t is the two-way travel time in seconds. In sea water c is about 1500 m/s. It varies with temperature, salinity and pressure, so use a measured value. The transducer sits a known draft below the water surface, so depth below the surface = d + draft.

items: Fix the boat position at every sounding.
Record depth, position and tide height.

blocks.text: This is the same travel-time idea as liDAR and laser scanning, with sound in water instead of light in air. Sounding lines are spaced so the bed is covered.

Bathymetry is water depth measurement. Depth needs a position. A sounding plan sets parallel runs across the area and cross lines to check coverage. GNSS fixes the boat; a total station fixes near-shore marks. Each sounding is stored as a triple: position, depth, time. The sounding plan spacing depends on map scale and the least depth expected.

Chart datum is a low-water reference, close to lowest astronomical tide. A chart shows depth below datum, not below the moving surface. Tide height h is the water level above chart datum at sounding time. The water surface is h above datum, so the charted (reduced) depth is D = depth below the surface − h. If the tide is below chart datum, h is negative and the charted depth is larger than the measured one. A tide gauge or predicted tide gives h.

A bathymetric chart plots reduced depth at position, with shoreline and symbols. Depth contours join equal reduced depths. Cross lines expose gaps and position errors. Dredging, navigation and reservoir capacity use the chart. Once the reduced depths are checked on the cross lines, the chart is drawn and contoured.

Fixing the boat. Today the boat is fixed by RTK GNSS on the transducer pole, or near the shore by a total station tracking a prism on the boat. Older methods, still asked in examinations, are a range line with a rope or wire marked at intervals, two angles measured with sextants from the boat to three shore stations, or angles from two shore theodolites. Sound speed is measured with a probe: an error from 1500 to 1520 m/s is 1.3 %, 0.40 m in 30 m.

Underground survey begins at surface control. GNSS or a total station gives coordinates and height at the shaft collar. Two plumb wires or a laser transfer a vertical line down the shaft. A gyrotheodolite, or the two wires, gives azimuth: the horizontal angle of a line measured clockwise from north. Check the transfer before extending the traverse.

An underground traverse starts at the shaft station. A total station measures angles and distances along the tunnel and carries coordinates to the face. The surveyor sets out the centreline and grade, the designed slope. Two headings meet at breakthrough; breakthrough error is the difference between the faces. Azimuth transfer error grows with distance, so check with cross headings.

Levels transfer by tape or laser; check against a surface benchmark. Traverse adjustment uses the same closing error and Bowditch ideas as a compass or theodolite traverse. Mine and tunnel work call this mine surveying or underground surveying. The surface benchmark controls tunnel level.

spec.aria: Section of water with the boat, the transducer 0.50 metres down, the chart datum 1.20 metres below the surface and depths of 30.00, 30.50 and 29.30 metres; section of a shaft with two plumb wires W1 and W2 and the first tunnel station S.

examples.question: An echo sounder whose transducer is 0.50 m below the water surface records a two-way travel time of 0.040 s. Sound speed in the water is 1500 m/s. The tide is 1.20 m above chart datum. Find the depth below the water surface and the reduced depth below chart datum.
steps: Depth below the transducer d = c × one-way time = 1500 × 0.020 = 30.00 m.
Depth below the water surface = d + draft = 30.00 + 0.50 = 30.50 m.
The surface stands 1.20 m above chart datum, so the bed is 30.50 − 1.20 = 29.30 m below datum.
Check: at a low water exactly on chart datum (h = 0) the sounder would read 29.30 m below the surface at this spot.
examples.answer: Depth below the water surface 30.50 m; reduced depth below chart datum 29.30 m.

examples.question: Two plumb wires W1 and W2 hang 4.000 m apart in a shaft. At the surface the azimuth of W1W2 is found as 47°15′20″ and W1 is at (E 5000.000 m, N 8000.000 m). Underground, the first tunnel station S lies on the line W1W2 produced, 12.000 m beyond W2. Find the coordinates of S, and the lateral error at a face 2000 m from the shaft if the transferred azimuth were 10″ wrong.
steps: Distance W1 to S = 4.000 + 12.000 = 16.000 m along azimuth 47°15′20″.
An azimuth error δ swings the tunnel line about the shaft: lateral error = L × δ (radians).

The short 4 m base between the wires is the weak link: a 1 mm error in the position of one wire alone turns the line by 0.001/4.000 rad = 52″, so the wires are steadied in oil and observed many times, or a gyrotheodolite checks the azimuth.
examples.answer: S = (E 5011.750 m, N 8010.860 m); a 10″ azimuth error gives about 0.10 m at 2000 m.

traps: Using t instead of t/2 gives double the depth.
Adding the tide when it is above chart datum. The surface is above datum, so subtract: D = depth below surface − h.
Mixing sound speed units, for example 1500 m/s with t in milliseconds.
Calling chart datum the sea surface; it is a fixed low-water reference.
Forgetting the transducer draft: the sounder measures from the transducer, not from the water surface.

quiz.q: What does an echo sounder measure directly?
Why is travel time divided by 2?
quiz.a: The pulse travels down and back; one-way path is half.

quiz.q: A sounder gives t = 0.060 s and c = 1500 m/s. Find depth.
Tide is −0.30 m relative to chart datum and the depth below the water surface is 12.0 m. Find the reduced depth.
quiz.a: D = 12.0 − (−0.30) = 12.3 m. The water is below datum, so the charted depth is larger than the measured depth.

quiz.q: Why transfer azimuth down a shaft?
quiz.a: The tunnel traverse must run in the same coordinate system and direction as the surface control. An azimuth error at the shaft swings the whole tunnel line: 10″ over 2 km moves the face 2000 × 10/206 265 = 0.097 m sideways.

quiz.q: Name two causes of tunnel breakthrough error.
quiz.a: Azimuth transfer error and traverse angle or distance error; shaft coordinate and level errors also count.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern hydrographic work uses multibeam echo sounders, side-scan sonar and inertial navigation to map many depths per second. Tunnel guidance uses gyrotheodolites, lasers and total stations linked to tunnel boring machines. Search terms: multibeam bathymetry, sound velocity profile, gyro orientation, tunnel breakthrough survey.
